## Why phase behaviour matters
Enthalpy depends on the phase of a substance, not just its temperature and pressure.

::: {.incremental}
- Recall: temperature, pressure, **phase**, solutions and reactions all change enthalpy.
- Water (and steam) is the workhorse fluid for energy balances.
- To find $H$ we need to know *what phase* we are in — and when it changes.
:::

## What is steam?
Steam is water in the **vapour** (gas) phase.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Below the boiling point, water is a **liquid**.
- Add enough energy and it **vaporises** into steam.
- The energy needed to change phase is the focus of the next summary.
:::

## The phases of water
A pure substance can exist as solid, liquid or vapour — and along certain lines, two or three phases coexist.

. . .

A **phase diagram** maps which phase is stable at each temperature and pressure.

## The P–T phase diagram
::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![The pressure–temperature phase diagram for water](figures/water_pt_diagram.svg){width=65% #fig-water_pt}
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- Areas = a single phase (solid, liquid, vapour).
- Lines = two phases coexist (fusion, vaporisation, sublimation).
- The lines meet at the **triple point**; the vaporisation line ends at the **critical point**.
:::

## Vapour pressure
At a given temperature, a liquid and its vapour reach equilibrium at a specific pressure — the **vapour pressure**.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- The vaporisation line on the P–T diagram *is* the vapour pressure curve.
- Vapour pressure rises with temperature.
- **Boiling** happens when the vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Key Term
**Vapour pressure** — the pressure at which a pure liquid and its vapour are in equilibrium at a given temperature.
:::
:::

## Saturation
Any point *on* the vaporisation curve is a **saturation** condition — liquid and vapour coexisting.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
- At a given pressure, the temperature on the curve is the **saturation temperature**, $T^{sat}$.
- At a given temperature, the pressure on the curve is the **saturation pressure**, $P^{sat}$.
:::

. . .

$T^{sat}$ and $P^{sat}$ are just the boiling point expressed two ways.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Key Terms
**Saturation temperature** ($T^{sat}$) — the boiling temperature of a liquid at a given pressure.
**Saturation pressure** ($P^{sat}$) — the vapour pressure at a given temperature; the pressure at which boiling occurs.
:::

## Saturated and superheated steam
::: {.incremental}
- **Saturated steam** — vapour sitting right at $T^{sat}$, on the edge of condensing.
- **Superheated steam** — vapour heated *above* $T^{sat}$ at that pressure.
- **Wet steam** — a mixture of saturated liquid and saturated vapour together.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Key Terms
**Saturated steam** — vapour at its saturation temperature.
**Superheated steam** — vapour at a temperature above its saturation temperature.
:::
:::

## Wet steam and quality
Wet steam is part liquid, part vapour. Its **quality** $x$ is the mass fraction that is vapour.

. . .

$$x = \frac{\text{mass of vapour}}{\text{total mass}}$$

::: {.incremental}
- $x = 0$ → saturated liquid.
- $x = 1$ → saturated (dry) vapour.
- $0 < x < 1$ → wet steam.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Key Term
**Quality** ($x$) — the mass fraction of a saturated liquid–vapour mixture that is vapour.
:::

## The P–V diagram
::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![The pressure–volume diagram for water](figures/water_pv_diagram.svg){width=60% #fig-water_pv}
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- The **vapour dome** encloses the two-phase (wet steam) region.
- Left edge = saturated liquid; right edge = saturated vapour; they meet at the **critical point**.
- Inside the dome, temperature and pressure are fixed together — only the quality changes.
:::

## The P–V–T surface
::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![The three-dimensional P–V–T surface for water](figures/water_pvt_surface.svg){width=55% #fig-water_pvt}
:::

The P–T and P–V diagrams are just **projections** of one 3D surface onto two of its axes.

## Triple point and the phase rule
Recall the Gibbs phase rule:

$$F = C - \pi + 2$$

For water, a single component, $C = 1$:

::: {.incremental}
- One phase ($\pi = 1$): $F = 2$ → an **area** (choose $T$ and $P$ freely).
- Two phases ($\pi = 2$): $F = 1$ → a **line** (fix $T$, and $P$ follows).
- Three phases ($\pi = 3$): $F = 0$ → a **point** — the **triple point** is fixed.
:::

## The triple point is fixed
With $F = 0$, the triple point of water occurs at exactly one temperature and pressure.

. . .

It is so reproducible that it was long used to *define* the temperature scale.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Key Terms
**Triple point** — the unique $T$ and $P$ at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist.
**Critical point** — the end of the vaporisation curve, above which liquid and vapour become indistinguishable.
:::

## The H–T diagram
::: {style="text-align:center;"}
![Specific enthalpy versus temperature at constant pressure](figures/water_ht_diagram.svg){width=60% #fig-water_ht}
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
- Heating liquid: enthalpy rises with temperature (**sensible heat**).
- At $T^{sat}$: a **flat step** — enthalpy jumps at constant temperature (**latent heat**).
- Heating vapour: enthalpy rises again (**sensible heat**).
:::

. . .

That flat step is the subject of the next summary.

## Summary
::: {.incremental}
- A phase diagram maps the stable phase at each $T$ and $P$.
- The vaporisation curve is the **vapour pressure** curve; points on it are **saturation** conditions.
- **Saturated**, **superheated** and **wet** steam are distinguished by where they sit relative to $T^{sat}$.
- The Gibbs phase rule explains why single phases are areas, saturation is a line, and the triple point is a point.
- The **H–T diagram** previews sensible + latent heat — the next summary.
:::
